Higher-Order Molecular Grammars for Generative and Foundation Models in Chemistry

Yiming Huang    Yujie Zeng Affiliation: School of Electronic Engineering and Computer Science, Queen Mary University of London, London, UK    Vijay Prakash Dwivedi Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, USA    Simone Foti Affiliation: Department of Computing, Imperial College London, London, UK    Jianmin Wang    Jure Leskovec Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, USA    Tolga Birdal Affiliation: Department of Integrative Biotechnology, Yonsei University, Incheon, Korea Affiliation: Emails: y.huang24@imperial.ac.uk, jmwang@yonsei.ac.kr, t.birdal@imperial.ac.uk
Abstract

Molecular learning models are strongly shaped by their underlying representations. Yet standard sequential and graph formalisms struggle to explicitly encode higher-order topology, such as ring systems and recurring motifs. Existing higher-order representations can capture these structures directly, but they are often computationally demanding and difficult to decode into valid molecules. Here, we introduce Higher-order Grammar Representation (HGR), a principled, topology-aware framework that lifts molecules to combinatorial complexes and parses each complex into a compact sequence of production rules under a context-free higher-order grammar. By serialising higher-order topology into rule sequences, HGR makes these structures directly compatible with standard sequence models, avoiding the computational overhead of explicit higher-order encodings while preserving topological expressiveness. To reduce benchmark bias towards simple ring systems, we construct RingDiv, a ring-enriched benchmark containing 1.18 million molecules, including the curated RingDiv300k subset, and introduce the ring diversity index (RDI) to quantify ring-system coverage. In molecular generation, HGR-based models uniquely combine 100% validity by construction with leading distributional alignment, ranking first in FCD on all five generation benchmarks. In representation learning, HGR-FM achieves the highest mean AUC across seven MoleculeNet benchmarks under both transfer protocols, improving on the strongest baseline by 8.3 and 3.3 AUC points under probing and full fine-tuning, respectively. Collectively, these results establish HGR as an efficient higher-order representation for molecular generation and transferable representation learning.

Main

Molecular representation is a cornerstone of computational chemistry and drug design, bridging the gap between chemical structures and their biological, chemical, or physical properties [1]. Effective representations enable efficient and precise navigation of chemical space and thus are essential for drug discovery tasks, including virtual screening, activity prediction, and scaffold hopping [2]. However, current molecular representations struggle to encode higher-order structural information, that is, relations involving more than two atoms or molecular substructures, for generation and other tasks [3, 4]. This limitation matters because many chemically important structures, including rings and functional groups, are intrinsically higher-order [5]. Ring systems constrain molecular shape and position substituents [6], whereas functional groups establish interaction sites through polarity, hydrogen bonding and acidity. Together, these higher-order units connect atom-level connectivity to meso-scale chemical organisation and, ultimately, molecule-level behaviour, including reactivity, metabolic stability and interactions with biological targets [7, 8]. Our statistical analysis further shows that ring-system usage is highly concentrated, with a small set recurring across many drug-like molecules. This concentration makes ring-system diversity tractable to model. Beyond chemistry, higher-order relations are increasingly studied across diverse contexts, including the neural population activity underlying spatial navigation [9], group hunting behaviours in ecological competitive networks [10], and recommendations from multiple friends in social networks [11]. Nevertheless, higher-order topology has often been encoded only implicitly, reduced to pairwise graphs, or treated as isolated motifs [5].

Formally, molecular representation refers to the process of encoding molecules into mathematical or computational formats that algorithms can process to model, analyse, and predict molecular behaviour. Broadly, representations fall into three categories: early atom-level linear representations, graph-based representations, and the emerging higher-order topological representations (Fig. 1b). In addition, there exist various non-invertible mappings, such as molecular fingerprints [12], which transform molecules into computationally convenient forms (e.g., vectors in feature space) but generally lack strict reversibility.

Simplified Molecular-Input Line-Entry System (SMILES) [13] remains one of the most widely used molecular representations, using parentheses and numbers to denote branching points and ring closures. Although compact and interpretable, SMILES is prone to generating invalid molecules due to inherent syntactic and semantic flaws. To mitigate these challenges, Self-Referencing Embedded Strings (SELFIES) [14] improve robustness and validity in deep generative models, albeit at the cost of simplicity, interpretability and compactness. With the rapid rise of large language models, sequence-based representations have regained attention in molecular modelling and drug discovery [15, 16]. However, such string-based representations still do not explicitly encode hierarchical or meso-scale molecular structure. Molecular graphs provide a direct representation of atoms and bonds, and graph neural networks (GNNs) have been widely used for molecular learning and generation [17, 18]. Despite these advances, GNNs face several limitations. Standard message-passing GNNs are bounded by the Weisfeiler–Lehman (WL) test [19]; deeper architectures can suffer from over-smoothing [20] and over-squashing [21], which hinder long-range dependency modelling; and simple non-learnable readout functions can constrain graph-level representations. More fundamentally, both sequence- and graph-based representations leave hierarchical higher-order topology implicit, limiting their ability to transfer across structure-sensitive tasks [22].

Recently, higher-order structures have gained increasing attention in molecular modelling because they expose multi-way molecular organisation in forms useful for interpretability, efficient modelling and synthetic-accessibility analysis [5, 23]. A natural entry point to higher-order molecular topology is the ring system. Rings provide basic molecular shape, tune rigidity and substituent geometry, and strongly influence global physicochemical and electronic properties. Improved synthetic methods and building-block availability further broaden accessible ring chemical space, often leveraging conformational constraints to enhance potency and selectivity [7, 24]. Indeed, only a small fraction of bioactive molecules lack rings, and the vast majority of FDA-approved small-molecule drugs contain at least one ring [8]. Moreover, molecules are inherently hierarchical [3]. The atom level encodes fine-grained local connectivity and semantic similarity. The meso-scale captures chemically meaningful substructures, such as rings, functional groups, linkers and pharmacophores, that act as property-determining “semantic units”. These units govern polarity, hydrogen bonding, acidity, reactivity and conformational rigidity, linking local chemistry to global topology. The molecule level then summarises the overall structural patterns. If a model relies only on single-level reconstruction or contrastive supervision, it can either overemphasize local validity while producing globally incoherent assemblies (e.g., implausible motif fusion/attachment) or preserve coarse global structure at the expense of chemically faithful local details, making it difficult to maintain local consistency and global stability simultaneously.

Motif-based representations provide one pragmatic route to capture such higher-order topology. They can be interpreted within a hypergraph framework, where each fragment is treated as a hyperedge connecting multiple atoms [25]. This shift from atom- to fragment-level units parallels the transition from character- to word-level representations in natural language processing, and can yield more compact and expressive molecular encodings. These approaches broadly fall into fragment-string and fragment-graph representations. Fragment-string methods represent molecules as sequences of substructure units, including SMILES Pair Encoding (SPE) [26], t-SMILES [1], Group SELFIES [27], and fragSMILES [28]. These methods preserve the convenience of string-based modelling by serialising substructures into a one-dimensional order, but relations among fragments remain implicit in the string syntax. Graph-based fragment methods instead operate on fragment graphs, including motif-assembly generators and graph grammars. For example, JT-VAE [29] first generates a tree and then expands selected nodes by attaching substructures from a learned vocabulary. HierVAE [30] follows the same vocabulary-based principle but uses a multiresolution representation to improve combinatorial attachment and generate larger molecules. Graph grammars [31, 32, 33, 34] represent graphs through derivations over reusable subgraph rules, making them the closest existing family to HGR among fragment-based methods. However, graph grammars often face a trade-off between rule expressiveness and reuse. Context-specific fragments yield sparse, long-tailed rule vocabularies, whereas generic fragments weaken chemically meaningful motif semantics. Taken together, these fragment-based representations capture multi-atom interactions by treating fragments as higher-order units, but they do not explicitly encode the hierarchical part-whole organisation linking atoms, motifs, ring systems and larger molecular structures.

Topological deep learning (TDL) offers a general route beyond sequence-, graph- and fragment-based representations by modelling multi-way relations with hypergraphs, simplicial complexes, cell complexes and combinatorial complexes [22, 35]. Such structures are typically encoded using families of incidence (boundary) matrices. Although this makes higher-order structure explicit, generating over such structures is difficult because the incidence relations across topological dimensions must remain mutually consistent. For example, a face generated in an edge–face incidence matrix is structurally inconsistent if its boundary edges are absent from the node–edge incidence matrix. Molecular generation with incidence-based representations must navigate both the vast chemical space and a space of possible higher-order incidence relations that grows combinatorially with molecular size. Together with the limitations of sequence-, graph- and fragment-based representations discussed above, these challenges reveal a common trade-off between explicit higher-order structure and computational tractability. Sequence and graph encodings leave higher-order topology implicit, fragment-based methods do not explicitly encode its hierarchy, and incidence-based encodings make scalable generation difficult. Resolving this trade-off calls for an expressive and lossless representation that remains computationally tractable for both molecular generation and property prediction.

In this work, we propose Higher-order Grammar Representation (HGR), a principled and lossless representation that converts hierarchical higher-order molecular topology into a compact sequence of production rules. The central idea of HGR is to (i) lift a molecular graph into a combinatorial complex whose cells correspond to hierarchical and higher-order (multi-atom) relations, then (ii) parse each molecular complex into a sequence of production rules via a bottom-up contraction procedure, thereby inducing a higher-order grammar that supports exact decoding. Intuitively, HGR treats molecules as assemblies of reusable higher-order structural “words”, while retaining the attachment information needed for exact reconstruction. Each lifted cell contributes one production-rule token, and the resulting ordered sequence preserves the complex’s hierarchy across atom, motif and molecule scales. This sequence formulation makes HGR compatible with mature sequence architectures while avoiding the combinatorial cost of generation over higher-order incidence matrices. To address rule explosion, we introduce two lifting schemes, Motif-Induced Grammar (MIG) and Ring Scaffold Grammar (RSG), which respectively simplify complex anchor interfaces and stabilise lifting around ring systems. Evaluating higher-order molecular representations also requires benchmarks that adequately cover complex ring systems, which are underrepresented in commonly used molecular generation datasets. We therefore construct RingDiv, a ring-enriched benchmark of 1.18 million molecules, together with its topology-balanced RingDiv300k subset, to evaluate molecular generation in ring-diverse chemical space.

In summary, we make five contributions: (i) Lifting. We introduce two data-driven lifting strategies that convert a molecular graph into a combinatorial complex while controlling boundary complexity and rule explosion. (ii) Higher-order grammar. We propose HGR, a grammar-induction framework that serialises a molecule’s hierarchical higher-order topology into a compact HGR string and enables exact reconstruction through deterministic reverse derivation. (iii) Structure-aware rule encoding. We initialise production-rule tokens with permutation-invariant structural descriptors, yielding rule embeddings that reflect topological similarity and generalise to unseen rules. (iv) Generative and transfer applications. We instantiate HGR in two complementary regimes: grammar-constrained molecular generation through VAE-prior sampling (HGR-VAE) or latent diffusion sampling (HGR-LDF), and foundation modelling (HGR-FM) for transferable representation learning. Both regimes operate on the same HGR representation, enabling reuse across generative and predictive tasks. (v) RingDiv benchmark. We construct RingDiv, a ring-enriched benchmark that mitigates the ring-system bias of existing datasets. Our evaluation yields three key insights: (i) the grammar-based generators are valid by construction and achieve strong chemical and graph-structural distributional alignment; (ii) the same representation is broadly transferable, letting a single pretrained model support multiple downstream tasks and improve property prediction; and (iii) ablations attribute these gains to the explicit encoding of hierarchical higher-order topology rather than to sequence modelling alone, identifying it as a useful inductive bias. Relative to our preliminary report [36], the present study substantially extends the generative framework by refining HGR-VAE and introducing latent diffusion sampling, together with a fuller methodological specification and broader evaluation across five molecular-generation benchmarks. We further provide a more detailed characterisation of RingDiv, expanded ablation studies, and analyses of chemical and topological generation fidelity.

Results

Higher-order grammar representation

Drug discovery requires efficient navigation of chemical space, where the number of drug-like molecules is estimated at 102310^{23}–106010^{60}, far beyond the reach of experimental and virtual screening [37]. By contrast, our statistical analysis shows that ring-system usage is highly concentrated: only 630 distinct ring systems are observed in DrugBank [38] (Fig. 2a). More broadly, chemically meaningful motifs such as ring systems and functional groups encode multi-way relations that pairwise edges alone cannot fully capture. We therefore represent each molecule with HGR (Fig. 1): starting from the molecular graph (Fig. 1a), we lift it into a combinatorial complex (CC, Fig. 1c) [35], a formalism that unifies graphs, hypergraphs, and simplicial and cell complexes, and serialise the complex into a compact string of reusable production-rule tokens (Fig. 1e). In this representation, cells encode multi-way relations and carry hierarchical ranks. The resulting HGR string preserves hierarchy and attachment information for exact decoding, making higher-order topology tractable for standard sequence models.

Lifting operation.

In topological deep learning, the conversion from a graph to a higher-order domain is known as lifting. We adopt data-driven lifting based on a motif vocabulary mined from the molecule library, where motifs are frequent recurrent subgraphs in the dataset. To ensure invertibility, each production rule records the lifted motif together with an ordered anchor interface, a fixed ordering of its external neighbours and boundary bonds that is retained when the motif is contracted. This interface fixes the boundary correspondence during decoding and thereby supports exact reconstruction of the lifted complex and its associated molecular graph. However, the rule corpus may expand when motifs with many anchors admit multiple ordered anchor interfaces, each potentially inducing a separate rule.

To balance expressivity and rule compactness, we instantiate two lifting schemes named by their induced grammars: Motif-Induced Grammar (MIG) and Ring Scaffold Grammar (RSG). Each variant η∈{MIG,RSG}\eta\in\{\mathrm{MIG},\mathrm{RSG}\} maps a molecular graph to a combinatorial complex 𝒞η\mathcal{C}_{\eta} and induces the corresponding grammar Γη\Gamma_{\eta}. They share a frequency-guided motif-merging step but differ in the subsequent constraints: MIG lifting adds an anchor-resolution stage that curbs anchor proliferation via best-first motif expansion, whereas RSG lifting further stabilises lifting for cyclic molecules through ring-system-aware merging, mitigating rule inflation from complex ring attachments. Formal definitions and implementation details are provided in Methods. Unless otherwise stated, the main experiments use RSG, which provided a favourable balance between construction efficiency, rule compactness and empirical performance in our comparisons. MIG is reported as a supplementary ablation. The lifted complex can be viewed as a hierarchical tree (Fig. 1c): leaves correspond to atomic micro-structures, whereas internal nodes capture higher-order meso-structures.

Higher-order grammar induction and derivation.

HGR serialises a lifted complex and its associated molecular graph as a compact sequence of reusable production-rule tokens. The sequence records a bottom-up contraction in which every child subtree precedes its parent, and the resulting derivation hierarchy explicitly describes how atoms form motifs and how these motifs assemble into the complete molecule. During parsing, each step contracts one cell into a fresh non-terminal symbol and records the corresponding expansion as a production rule with an ordered interface graph and a local structural pattern (Fig. 1d). Parsing continues until the full structure is contracted to a single root non-terminal, which is designated as the start symbol SS. Across the molecular library, structurally identical contractions are assigned the same production rule, so induction collects only the distinct rules in a shared corpus (Fig. 1d). Applying the recorded rules in reverse losslessly reconstructs the original complex and associated molecular graph (Fig. 1f). Formal definitions and details are provided in Methods.

Whereas the shift from sequential representations to graph representations has advanced molecular machine learning, HGR takes a further leap by explicitly incorporating hierarchical higher-order structures. This rank-aware construction lets a single HGR string span atoms, motifs and ring systems. HGR offers three practical advantages: production rules encode reusable and interpretable higher-order motifs; grammar induction from real molecular complexes preserves valency and bonding constraints, ensuring chemical validity; and the representation supports exact reconstruction and assembly of new molecules.

Grammar compactness and rule reuse.

We next quantify how the lifting variants shape grammar complexity and rule reuse on ZINC250k [39], with additional results provided in Fig. 4. As more molecules are added during induction, the corpus size (unique production rules) grows sublinearly with dataset size and approaches saturation, with MIG and RSG converging to substantially more compact corpora than the Molecular Hypergraph Grammar (MHG) baseline [31] (Fig. 2b). Consistently, MIG and RSG exhibit markedly more balanced rule-frequency distributions, attenuating the long tail of rarely used rules and increasing overall rule reuse (Fig. 2c).

RingDiv: a ring-diversity benchmark

Beyond representation design, rigorous evaluation requires benchmarks that cover ring-rich chemical space. Conventional molecular generation benchmarks underrepresent ring-system diversity, creating a mismatch with modern drug-discovery chemistry, where fused, bridged and multi-ring architectures are increasingly relevant [8]. This mismatch can distort evaluation by favouring models that fit simplified benchmark distributions while leaving their behaviour in ring-diverse chemical space unresolved. Results on QM9 and MOSES (Sec. 4.2) further show that modern generators already approach empirical reference levels on conventional benchmarks with simpler ring-system profiles, leaving little headroom to stress-test models or identify practical routes for improvement.

We therefore constructed RingDiv, a benchmark of 1.18 million molecules explicitly enriched for diverse ring systems. RingDiv300k was then derived from RingDiv as a topology-balanced development subset of 299,819 molecules. The construction began with approximately 143 million compounds from PubChem, SureChEMBL and five commercial screening libraries. After deduplication, these compounds were merged into a candidate corpus. Molecules in this corpus were then annotated by ring size and fusion pattern, with macrocycles excluded to keep the benchmark focused on drug-like ring diversity. We then applied quota-first sampling to enrich rare but informative ring topologies (e.g., medium rings, spirocyclic and bridged systems), followed by MaxMin selection over Morgan fingerprints to preserve overall structural diversity and suppress near-duplicates (see Methods and Sec. 2.2).

To quantify ring-system coverage relative to standard generation benchmarks, we introduce the Ring Diversity Index (RDI), a ratio-based measure of ring-system coverage per molecule:

RDI=#​Unique Ring Systems#​Molecules.\text{RDI}=\frac{\#\,\text{Unique Ring Systems}}{\#\,\text{Molecules}}. (1)

As shown in Fig. 3a, RingDiv300k and RingDiv exhibit higher RDI than most benchmarks. Fig. 3b complements the ratio-based RDI with absolute counts of unique ring systems, showing broader ring-topology coverage in the RingDiv variants.

Because RDI captures dataset-level coverage rather than per-molecule complexity, we complemented it with the Quantitative Ring Complexity Index (QRCI) [40] and separately examined ring-category prevalence and the unique-scaffold ratio. Higher QRCI values indicate greater ring-system complexity and topological diversity. The QRCI distributions of RingDiv300k and RingDiv are concentrated towards the upper end of the approved-drug range (QRCI = 1.8–5), indicating enrichment for greater ring complexity without a shift into the overcomplex regime. RingDiv300k and RingDiv show higher prevalences of medium rings and spirocyclic, fused and bridged ring systems than most benchmarks (Fig. 3d). They also have the two highest unique-scaffold ratios. Across the evaluated benchmarks, RingDiv and RingDiv300k combine broad ring-system coverage with relatively high per-molecule ring complexity and enrichment of uncommon ring topologies.

Molecular generation with HGR

Equipped with the HGR representation and the ring-enriched RingDiv benchmark, we first turn to molecular generation, a core drug-discovery task that supplies novel candidates and shapes downstream screening quality [2]. However, current molecular generative models predominantly rely on sequence- or graph-based representations that emphasize local features such as atoms and bonds but fail to capture intrinsic higher-order molecular topology. Despite recent advances in topology-aware generation [23], direct generation of higher-order structures remains elusive. The difficulty stems from the combinatorial higher-order search space and the need to maintain consistency across incidence relations [22].

To close this gap, we represent molecules as expressive HGR strings, whose rule tokens make higher-order topology explicit. This recasts molecular generation as sequence modelling, allowing standard sequence generative models to operate on higher-order molecular structure. Specifically, we adopt a Grammar Variational Autoencoder (GVAE) [41] tailored to the induced grammar, whose decoder restricts generation to admissible HGR strings while its latent space captures semantically meaningful variations in molecular topology. Following training, molecular generation proceeds via two parallel routes: (i) direct sampling from the latent space to obtain latent codes (HGR-VAE), or (ii) latent-space diffusion to synthesize latent codes (HGR-LDF). The grammar decoder then maps the resulting latent codes to molecular structures. HGR-based generation produces molecular combinatorial complexes that retain hierarchical higher-order topology, together with associated molecular graphs recovered from the recorded rule interfaces. Because the production rules are derived from subgraphs of real molecules, rule application preserves recorded bonds and ordered anchor interfaces, yielding valency-preserving decoding by construction. For each generated molecule, the corresponding rule sequence records how reusable higher-order rules assemble the final structure. The representation therefore preserves local chemical constraints while recording higher-order structure and its assembly trajectory.

To assess generation performance, we compared HGR-based generators with representative diffusion-based, higher-order-aware and sequence-control baselines on GuacaMol and RingDiv300k, two larger and more discriminative benchmarks (Tab. 1). SELFIES-VAE [14] serves as a syntax-valid sequence representation control in the main comparison. Consistent with our valency-preserving design, both HGR-VAE and HGR-LDF achieved 100% RDKit validity on all five generation benchmarks. HGR-LDF showed strong distributional alignment, achieving the best FCD score on GuacaMol (84.4 versus 78.3 for the strongest diffusion baseline) and the lowest FCD and best KL score on RingDiv300k (0.4652 and 99.2). HGR-VAE ranked second by FCD on both benchmarks. SELFIES-VAE also achieved 100% validity but showed weaker distributional alignment on RingDiv300k (FCD 2.4266; KL score 92.8). HGR is thus the only representation that combines full validity with leading chemical-distribution alignment. One exception in the main comparison is the GuacaMol KL score, where HGR-LDF trails the strongest diffusion baselines.

Extended results in Sec. 4.2 support this interpretation across additional datasets, baselines and structural metrics. Among these structural checks, NSPDK MMD is used as a secondary structural-distribution metric, and curvature-filtration descriptors are reported as auxiliary metrics. SMILES-VAE reached competitive distributional scores only at substantially lower validity, highlighting the need for a validity-preserving representation. HGR-based generators also achieved lower FCD and NSPDK MMD than MHG-VAE, the closest molecular hypergraph grammar baseline. Within HGR, RSG generally improved topology-distribution alignment over MIG, indicating that ring-system-aware grammar construction contributes to generation quality. These extended benchmarks further show that QM9 and MOSES are close to saturation, underscoring the need for more discriminative benchmarks like RingDiv. Beyond generation quality, HGR-VAE trained fastest on all five benchmarks and sampled in minutes rather than the hours required by diffusion baselines (Tab. 13).

To test whether generated molecules retain chemically meaningful substructures, we profiled each molecule against a predefined functional-group panel and recorded the fraction of molecules containing each group (SMARTS definitions and procedure in Sec. 3.2). This local-composition analysis shows that both HGR generation routes preserve the broad functional-group profile of the RingDiv300k reference test set (Fig. 4a,b). Nitrogen-containing groups and aromatic motifs showed the closest agreement, with the dominant pyridine essentially reproduced and most groups agreeing to within about one percentage point. HGR-LDF further reduced the ether enrichment observed under HGR-VAE. Residual deviations were confined to a few motifs: benzene and carbonyl-containing groups such as amides and ketones were enriched, whereas thioethers, cyclopropanes, epoxides and rare aldehydes were under-represented. Overall, grammar-constrained generation preserves the major functional-group composition of the reference set, although a few motif-level deviations remain.

We next assessed whether this fidelity persisted across molecular size by binning molecules by heavy-atom count and measuring per-bin agreement with the test set (Fig. 4c–e). For the ring-size distribution (Fig. 4c), both HGR variants stayed close to the train-versus-test floor at all sizes (JS ≤0.01\leq 0.01). By contrast, the graph-diffusion baselines showed larger deviations on large molecules, with DiGress rising about tenfold to JS ≈0.09\approx 0.09 above 45 heavy atoms. The ranking differed for functional-group composition (Fig. 4d): the ring-specialist HoG-Diff and DeFoG were less accurate (JS ≈0.02−0.03\approx 0.02-0.03), whereas HGR remained low (JS ≈0.01−0.015\approx 0.01-0.015) and comparable to the most accurate baseline, DiGress. HGR showed the most consistent agreement with the reference across both ring topology and local composition. Because ring-rich molecules can be synthetically challenging, we next examined size-resolved synthetic accessibility [44] (Fig. 4e). HGR-generated molecules retained low SA scores across the size range, whereas diffusion baselines became less accessible with size, with DiGress reaching SA ≈6\approx 6. Together, the size-resolved analysis shows that grammar-constrained generation preserves chemical fidelity and synthetic feasibility on large, ring-rich molecules for which graph-diffusion models showed larger deviations.

We further compared chemical-space coverage using two-dimensional Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) [45] density maps of Morgan fingerprints [12] (Fig. 4f). Because Morgan fingerprints encode local substructures, these density maps provide a compact and intuitive comparison of reference and generated chemical-space distributions. The HGR variants showed broad overlap with the test-set density, whereas the diffusion baselines showed more restricted or shifted density patterns.

Molecular foundation model with HGR

Beyond generation, the same HGR string can serve as the substrate for a foundation model. Molecular foundation models (FMs) pretrained on large corpora can learn transferable representations for downstream tasks with limited task-specific supervision [46, 47, 48]. However, current molecular FMs largely depend on SMILES strings[46, 47], molecular graphs[49, 48, 50], or simple combinations of the two[51]. These SMILES- and graph-centred inputs mainly encode atomic connectivity, leaving hierarchical higher-order patterns underrepresented. Simply scaling models on such inputs is therefore unlikely to overcome this representational bottleneck, limiting their potential in chemistry and drug discovery [4].

To address these gaps, we propose an HGR-based molecular foundation model (HGR-FM) (Fig. 5a) that uses compact HGR strings as structurally expressive inputs and is pretrained for multi-task transfer. Each rule token is initialised with a structure-derived embedding from Weisfeiler-Lehman (WL) label histograms. This embedding is permutation-invariant and generalises to unseen rules. A Grammar Transformer then encodes these token embeddings into contextualized representations. Because vanilla Transformers do not exploit hierarchical or topological structure by default, we introduce a higher-order position encoding implemented as a composite attention bias. This bias injects cues for cell rank, grammar-tree distance and relation type, together with pairwise molecular connectivity, into the pre-softmax attention logits. Contextualized atom-level token states support atom-level prediction, whereas the final hidden state of the molecule-level token serves as a fixed-length molecular fingerprint. Finally, multi-level pretext tasks align atom-, fragment-, molecule- and conformation-level signals, with shallow task-specific multilayer perceptron (MLP) heads projecting the corresponding representations to their training targets. Model architecture, rule-token initialisation and pretraining objectives are detailed in Sec. 1.6.

After pretraining, we evaluated HGR-FM across various unseen downstream tasks using two standard transfer protocols: full fine-tuning and probing. Performance was reported as AUC (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve), following the MoleculeNet convention. Across seven MoleculeNet benchmarks (BBBP, Tox21, ToxCast, SIDER, ClinTox, HIV and BACE) [52], HGR-FM achieved the highest average AUC under both transfer protocols (Fig. 5b). At the task level, HGR-FM led all seven benchmarks under probing and six under full fine-tuning, with SIDER as the only exception. The largest probing gain was observed on ClinTox (89.7 versus 63.5 for the strongest external baseline). Complete task-level probing and full fine-tuning results are provided in Tab. 12. Comparing the two transfer protocols, probing approached or surpassed full fine-tuning (Fig. 5d). This pattern may reflect full fine-tuning’s instability on small downstream datasets: updating the pretrained encoder can induce representation drift, whereas freezing it acts as an implicit regularizer. The narrow gap between probing and fine-tuning indicates that the pretrained encoder learns semantically rich and transferable representations from which shallow prediction heads can read out task-relevant features.

To isolate the source of these gains, we ablated the two HGR-specific components, first removing higher-order tokens from the HGR string to leave only atom-level tokens. Experimental results show that higher-order rule tokens are important for the observed gains: removing them degraded pretraining dynamics, yielding consistently higher validation loss and a clear drop in downstream mean AUC (Fig. 5c). Disabling the attention bias also degraded performance, but the effect was smaller than that of removing higher-order rule tokens. These results support the core design premise: tokenizing molecules with higher-order rules exposes meso-scale and global structural cues to the Transformer, letting it learn representations that go beyond atom-level co-occurrence and better reflect hierarchical molecular topology.

We next assessed the impact of pretraining data by comparing models trained on RingDiv, ZINC2m and their combination (Fig. 5e). ZINC2m mainly comprises simpler molecular structures that capture fundamental chemical patterns and suffice for many benchmark tasks, whereas RingDiv contributes more complex and topologically rich molecules that broaden the model’s exposure to higher-order structures. Combining ZINC2m with RingDiv yielded the best downstream performance, highlighting the value of larger and structurally broader pretraining data.

Together, these results show that HGR-FM integrates symbolic production rules with explicit structural inductive biases to produce transferable and chemically informed representations. Its strong probing performance shows that grammar-informed pretraining learns task-relevant molecular features efficiently, positioning HGR-FM as a promising foundation model framework for molecular representation learning.

Discussion

This work bridges topological deep learning and sequence modelling by encoding hierarchical molecular topology as a decodable string that standard sequence models can learn from. Building on a combinatorial-complex view of molecules, we examined three linked aspects: reusable grammar induction, ring-diverse benchmarking, and HGR-based generation and foundation modelling. These analyses show that explicit higher-order topology can support chemically valid generation, improve distributional alignment on ring-diverse chemical space, and yield transferable molecular representations. Ablations that remove the higher-order rule tokens, leaving only atom-level tokens, degrade transfer (Fig. 5c), indicating that the gains stem from higher-order topology rather than from atom-level co-occurrence alone.

Conventional molecular benchmarks underrepresent complex ring systems, whereas modern drug discovery increasingly involves fused, bridged and multi-ring architectures. This imbalance can hamper generalisation to ring-diverse chemical space. Performance saturation on conventional benchmarks can also mask methodological differences that surface only under more discriminative evaluation. RingDiv and HGR address the two sides of this gap: RingDiv enriches evaluation with 1.18 million ring-diverse molecules, and HGR converts molecular combinatorial complexes into production-rule sequences that can be modelled by standard sequence architectures. In particular, HGR contrasts with incidence-matrix encodings of higher-order topology, which represent structure explicitly but can make molecular generation computationally costly. Together, RingDiv and HGR pair a more demanding evaluation regime with a representation that exposes reusable higher-order motifs for generation and transfer learning.

The present study also identifies several practical limitations of HGR and its current evaluation. Computationally, the lifting step is the main upfront cost for very large corpora, although it runs once, parallelises well and is amortised across subsequent training and generation. This cost is further mitigated downstream, as compact HGR strings enable HGR-VAE to train and sample faster than the diffusion baselines. Generation remains sensitive to local chemical composition, with motif-level biases such as ether enrichment under direct latent sampling. Latent-space diffusion reduced this enrichment, and the remaining distributional gaps identify motifs for which grammar-constrained sampling could be improved. Finally, the generated molecules and predicted candidates remain computational proposals until prospective wet-lab assays establish their practical value. Beyond addressing these boundaries, future work can extend HGR to other chemical tasks. For instance, localised edits to HGR rules could support molecular editing, while substituting rules that encode core ring systems could enable scaffold hopping.

Beyond these specific tasks, HGR offers a reusable structural vocabulary that makes the higher-order topology of molecules explicit and learnable by encoding how local chemical units assemble into meso-scale motifs and whole-molecule architectures. RingDiv provides a benchmark for evaluating molecular models on complex, ring-rich chemistry. More broadly, this work suggests a route towards applying LLM-style sequence models to graph- and topology-centric scientific domains by serialising higher-order structures into production-rule sequences.

Methods

Preliminaries and problem formulation

We introduce the HGR string as a compact, invertible sequence representation of higher-order molecular topology. Starting from a molecular graph 𝒢\mathcal{G}, we first lift it to a combinatorial complex 𝒞\mathcal{C} that encodes hierarchical higher-order structure. Grammar induction then uses both 𝒞\mathcal{C} and 𝒢\mathcal{G} to produce an HGR string 𝒓\bm{r}.

A molecule can be represented as a graph 𝒢=(𝒱,ℰ)\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E}), with atoms as vertices 𝒱\mathcal{V} and covalent bonds as edges ℰ\mathcal{E}. However, molecules often contain multi-way relations such as rings, functional groups and other higher-order motifs that pairwise edges cannot fully capture [5, 8, 25]. We therefore represent a molecule as a combinatorial complex (CC) [35], a general formalism that unifies graphs, simplicial and cell complexes, and hypergraphs within a single framework. A CC is a triple

𝒞=(𝒱,𝒳,rk),\mathcal{C}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{X},\operatorname{rk}), (2)

where 𝒱\mathcal{V} is a finite set of vertices, 𝒳⊆Pow⁡(𝒱)∖{∅}\mathcal{X}\subseteq\operatorname{Pow}(\mathcal{V})\setminus\{\emptyset\} is a collection of non-empty subsets called cells (or relations), and rk:𝒳→ℤ≥0\operatorname{rk}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} is a rank function. The structure satisfies two conditions: every singleton {v}\{v\} is a cell with rk⁡({v})=0\operatorname{rk}(\{v\})=0, so atoms have rank 00; and rk\operatorname{rk} is order-preserving, i.e. x⊆y⇒rk⁡(x)≤rk⁡(y)x\subseteq y\Rightarrow\operatorname{rk}(x)\leq\operatorname{rk}(y). In HGR, the lifted CC encodes the higher-order hierarchy, while the molecular graph 𝒢\mathcal{G} supplies the pairwise adjacency used during rule construction; the two roles stay separate throughout.

Molecular lifting algorithms

We now specify how molecular graphs are lifted into combinatorial complexes. Let 𝒢=(𝒱,ℰ)\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E}) be a molecular graph and let ℳ\mathcal{M} denote the motif vocabulary mined from a molecule library. For each lifting variant η∈{MIG,RSG}\eta\in\{\mathrm{MIG},\mathrm{RSG}\}, molecular lifting defines a fixed, data-driven structural map

Λη:(𝒢,ℳ)⟼𝒞η=(𝒱,𝒳η,rkη),\Lambda_{\eta}:(\mathcal{G},\mathcal{M})\longmapsto\mathcal{C}_{\eta}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{X}_{\eta},\operatorname{rk}_{\eta}), (3)

where 𝒳η\mathcal{X}_{\eta} is the cell family recorded by the lifting hierarchy, containing singleton atom cells and the lifted motif cells produced by merging. The molecular graph 𝒢\mathcal{G} is retained alongside 𝒞η\mathcal{C}_{\eta} and later supplies the pairwise adjacency used to define the anchor interfaces and local rule graphs.

Both lifting variants are built on a frequency-guided motif-merging backbone. Starting from singleton atom cells, the algorithm scores adjacent candidate subgraphs by their frequency and merges the highest-frequency non-overlapping candidates in parallel, yielding progressively coarser motif cells. The merges form a contraction tree whose leaves are atom cells. For any cell σ\sigma, its rank rkη⁡(σ)\operatorname{rk}_{\eta}(\sigma) is defined as its height in this tree, namely the maximum number of edges from σ\sigma to an atom leaf. This definition assigns rank 00 to atom cells and makes rank non-decreasing under cell inclusion: σ⊆τ\sigma\subseteq\tau implies rkη⁡(σ)≤rkη⁡(τ)\operatorname{rk}_{\eta}(\sigma)\leq\operatorname{rk}_{\eta}(\tau).

A key practical challenge is controlling the number of boundary anchors and the resulting attachment complexity. For a merged cell σ\sigma, its anchors are the external neighbours of σ\sigma in the molecular graph 𝒢\mathcal{G}. More anchors give rise to more attachment configurations and can inflate the induced rule corpus. The two lifting variants specialise this shared backbone in different ways. MIG adds anchor resolution to simplify complex interfaces, whereas RSG stages merging and anchor resolution around ring systems to preserve them as coherent higher-order units during lifting.

MIG lifting.

MIG is designed to reduce excessive anchors. When a merged motif exposes an ambiguous interface, defined here as more than two anchors, MIG expands the motif by absorbing neighbouring subgraphs in a best-first manner, prioritising higher-frequency motifs. This absorption continues until the interface becomes unambiguous. MIG typically decreases the number of induced rules, at the cost of producing slightly larger motifs. The merging procedure and its anchor-resolution subroutine are summarised in Supplementary Algorithm 1.

RSG lifting.

RSG further stabilises lifting in cyclic chemistry by prioritising ring-system-aware merges. It first identifies rings using the smallest set of smallest rings decomposition and groups rings that share atoms into common ring systems. RSG then applies constrained merging in stages. Non-ring regions are first merged to consolidate acyclic fragments; side chains that attach uniquely to a ring system are absorbed into that system; within-system merges are prioritised before cross-system merging is allowed to preserve ring coherence; and each ring system is treated as a unit for anchor resolution, allowing necessary neighbouring vertices to be absorbed while keeping the interface manageable. A final global merging pass is then applied. This staged design yields a more consistent hierarchy for ring-rich molecules and mitigates rule inflation caused by complex ring attachments.

Higher-order grammar induction and derivation

Intuitively, a terminal symbol denotes an observed atom-level object, whereas a non-terminal symbol marks a replaceable site corresponding to a contracted cell. A production rule rewrites a non-terminal site into a local structure when its left-hand-side anchor interface matches the site’s interface. Formally, the grammar is Γ=(Σ,𝒩,S,𝒫)\Gamma=(\Sigma,\mathcal{N},{S},\mathcal{P}), where Σ\Sigma and 𝒩\mathcal{N} denote the finite sets of terminal and non-terminal symbols, respectively, S∈𝒩{S}\in\mathcal{N} is the start symbol, and 𝒫={r1,r2,…,r|𝒫|}\mathcal{P}=\{r_{1},r_{2},\dots,r_{|\mathcal{P}|}\} is the corpus of production rules. For each complex produced by either lifting variant, parsing returns an ordered HGR string 𝒓\bm{r} of rule tokens drawn from 𝒫\mathcal{P}. Across the library, induction accumulates the rules created during parsing into the production-rule corpus 𝒫\mathcal{P}. The reverse direction, derivation, rebuilds a complex from the start symbol SS. The overall induction-derivation workflow is illustrated in Fig. 1.

Production-rule construction.

We consider parsing a single lifted complex 𝒞\mathcal{C} paired with its molecular graph 𝒢\mathcal{G}. Rank-zero cells correspond to atoms, whereas higher-rank cells are the internal nodes of the contraction tree. We serialise this hierarchy in a bottom-up post-order, completing each child subtree before its parent cell, with admissible sibling-subtree orders defined in Supplementary Methods. Following the selected order, we contract each cell σ∈𝒳\sigma\in\mathcal{X} into a fresh site marked by the non-terminal symbol N∗N^{*}, producing one rule token rir_{i} for the HGR string. After rir_{i} is recorded, N∗N^{*} represents σ\sigma in the current complex and graph, reducing the active structure while allowing this site to participate in subsequent contractions. Repeating this contraction step reduces the structure to a single root site, which is marked by the start symbol S{S}.

Each production rule ri:𝒢iL→𝒢iRr_{i}:\mathcal{G}^{L}_{i}\to\mathcal{G}^{R}_{i} comprises a left-hand-side interface graph and a right-hand-side local graph (Fig. 1d). The ordered anchor interface specifies both whether the rule is applicable and how its local rewrite attaches to the surrounding graph. We define the anchor set as

𝒱ancσ={v∈𝒱∖σ∣∃u∈σ​ s.t. ​(u,v)∈ℰ}.\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{anc}}^{\sigma}=\{v\in\mathcal{V}\setminus\sigma\mid\exists u\in\sigma\text{ s.t. }(u,v)\in\mathcal{E}\}. (4)

Its canonical ordering and corresponding boundary-bond attributes define the ordered anchor interface. When σ\sigma is contracted, this interface is retained at the site marked by N∗N^{*}, thereby fixing the attachment correspondence for reverse derivation. Accordingly, the left-hand side is the star-shaped interface graph

𝒢iL=({N∗}∪𝒱ancσ,{(N∗,v)∣v∈𝒱ancσ}),\mathcal{G}^{L}_{i}=\left(\{N^{*}\}\cup\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{anc}}^{\sigma},\{(N^{*},v)\mid v\in\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{anc}}^{\sigma}\}\right), (5)

where the anchor ordering and boundary-bond attributes are retained on the incident edges.

Let 𝒢~=(𝒱~,ℰ~)\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}=(\widetilde{\mathcal{V}},\widetilde{\mathcal{E}}) denote the working graph at the current contraction step and σ~⊆𝒱~\widetilde{\sigma}\subseteq\widetilde{\mathcal{V}} the current representation of σ\sigma. For U⊆𝒱~U\subseteq\widetilde{\mathcal{V}}, we write 𝒢~[U]=(U,{(u,v)∈ℰ~∣u,v∈U})\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}[U]=(U,\{(u,v)\in\widetilde{\mathcal{E}}\mid u,v\in U\}) for the subgraph induced by UU, with all vertex and edge attributes inherited from 𝒢~\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}. The corresponding production rule has right-hand side

𝒢iR=𝒢~​[σ~∪𝒱ancσ].\mathcal{G}^{R}_{i}=\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}\bigl[\widetilde{\sigma}\cup\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{anc}}^{\sigma}\bigr]. (6)

Thus, 𝒢iR\mathcal{G}^{R}_{i} records the local structure replaced by N∗N^{*}: the atoms and child non-terminal sites currently representing σ\sigma, together with the boundary bonds connecting this representation to the ordered anchors. Structurally identical local contractions reuse the same production rule in 𝒫\mathcal{P}. Together, the rule order in the HGR string and the ordered child non-terminal sites in each 𝒢iR\mathcal{G}^{R}_{i} specify the derivation tree used for reverse reconstruction.

Reverse derivation and lossless reconstruction.

Given the induced grammar Γ\Gamma and an HGR string 𝒓\bm{r}, reverse derivation reconstructs the combinatorial complex and associated molecular graph (Fig. 1f). Because the HGR string is stored in post-order, reverse derivation starts from S{S} and consumes rev⁡(𝒓)\operatorname{rev}(\bm{r}), beginning with the root rule and proceeding towards the leaves. At each step, the current rule rir_{i} expands the non-terminal site at the top of the decoder’s last-in-first-out (LIFO) stack, which selects the rewrite site without global subgraph-isomorphism search. The rule rewrites 𝒢iL\mathcal{G}^{L}_{i} into 𝒢iR\mathcal{G}^{R}_{i} and reconnects boundary bonds through the ordered anchor interface, which fixes the boundary correspondence even for symmetric intermediates. Thus, reverse derivation losslessly restores both the input lifted complex 𝒞m\mathcal{C}_{m} and its associated molecular graph 𝒢m\mathcal{G}_{m} (Supplementary Proposition 1).

Rule-token initialisation.

For use with neural models, each production-rule token in the HGR string is mapped to an input vector. Rather than one-hot rule identifiers, which treat rules as unrelated symbols, we initialise each rule token rir_{i} from a structure-aware Weisfeiler–Lehman (WL) histogram of its right-hand-side graph 𝒢iR\mathcal{G}^{R}_{i}. The WL histogram iteratively relabels each atom by combining its attributes with the sorted labels of its neighbours. Pooling the resulting labels yields a fixed-length, permutation-invariant feature that generalises to rules unseen during training. These WL features already give distinct initialisations to more than 98%98\% of production rules. In HGR-FM, these features are augmented with a random-walk encoding, so the combined embedding distinguishes all rules in our grammars. Full construction and model-specific initialisers are detailed in Sec. 1.4.

HGR-based generative models

With the induced grammar and its rule-token initialisation in hand, we build a grammar VAE over HGR strings, together with an optional latent-diffusion sampler over its latent space.

Grammar variational autoencoder (GVAE).

The GVAE consists of an encoder–decoder pair that operates on grammar production rules rather than atomic tokens [41]. Given a molecular combinatorial complex 𝒞\mathcal{C}, we first parse it into an HGR string 𝒓\bm{r} whose rule tokens are drawn from the production rule corpus 𝒫\mathcal{P}. Each rule token is then mapped to its WL-based embedding, so that the symbolic string 𝒓\bm{r} becomes a sequence of fixed-length feature vectors. From this feature sequence, the encoder produces a latent variable 𝒛∈ℝd\bm{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, parameterising the variational posterior qϕ​(𝒛∣𝒓)q_{\bm{\phi}}(\bm{z}\mid\bm{r}). The latent prior is an isotropic Gaussian, p⁡(𝒛)=𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝑰)p(\bm{z})=\mathcal{N}(\bm{0},\bm{I}). Conditioned on 𝒛\bm{z}, the decoder represents p𝜽​(𝒓∣𝒛)p_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{r}\mid\bm{z}) using an autoregressive factorization over rev⁡(𝒓)\operatorname{rev}(\bm{r}), beginning with the root rule and proceeding towards the leaves under grammar constraints.

The model is trained with a β\beta-VAE style evidence lower bound over the dataset of HGR strings [53]:

ℒGVAE(𝜽,ϕ;𝒓)=𝔼qϕ​(𝒛∣𝒓)[logp𝜽(𝒓∣𝒛)]−βKL(qϕ(𝒛∣𝒓)∥p(𝒛)).\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GVAE}}(\bm{\theta},\bm{\phi};\bm{r})=\mathbb{E}_{q_{\bm{\phi}}(\bm{z}\mid\bm{r})}[\log p_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{r}\mid\bm{z})]-\beta\,\mathrm{KL}\!\left(q_{\bm{\phi}}(\bm{z}\mid\bm{r})\,\|\,p(\bm{z})\right). (7)

The reconstruction term encourages recovery of the input HGR string, whereas the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence regularises the latent space; β\beta controls the trade-off between reconstruction fidelity and latent regularisation. Variable-length sequences are padded to a common length with a special padding token for mini-batch training.

Grammar-constrained decoding.

To ensure syntactic validity, decoding is guided by a last-in-first-out (LIFO) stack of pending non-terminal sites. At step tt, the stack top selects the site αt\alpha_{t} to expand. A production rule is admissible only if its ordered anchor interface matches the interface at αt\alpha_{t}. The decoder outputs an unnormalized logit vector 𝒍t∈ℝ|𝒫|\bm{l}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{P}|}, and a binary mask 𝒎αt∈{0,1}|𝒫|\bm{m}_{\alpha_{t}}\in\{0,1\}^{|\mathcal{P}|} encodes rule admissibility. The probability of selecting rule rir_{i} given the preceding rules 𝒓<t\bm{r}_{<t}, αt\alpha_{t} and the latent variable 𝒛\bm{z} is

p⁡(rt=ri∣𝒓<t,αt,𝒛)=𝒎αt,i​exp⁡(𝒍t,i)∑j𝒎αt,j​exp⁡(𝒍t,j).p(r_{t}=r_{i}\mid\bm{r}_{<t},\alpha_{t},\bm{z})=\frac{\bm{m}_{\alpha_{t},i}\exp(\bm{l}_{t,i})}{\sum_{j}\bm{m}_{\alpha_{t},j}\exp(\bm{l}_{t,j})}. (8)

After a rule is selected, its child non-terminal sites are pushed onto the stack in reverse of their stored order. Decoding continues until the stack is empty or the dataset-specific maximum sequence length is reached. Sequences with non-empty stacks at this limit are discarded as incomplete derivations. Each completed derivation is therefore grammar-valid and satisfies the local valency and bonding constraints encoded by the induced rules, without post-hoc filtering for these constraints.

Latent diffusion sampling.

To further improve sample quality, we model the GVAE latent distribution with a standard score-based diffusion model [54, 55]. Latent codes are perturbed by a forward stochastic differential equation (SDE) and recovered by the corresponding reverse-time SDE, whose score function is trained by denoising score matching [56]. We adopt this framework without modification and provide the full formulation in Sec. 1.5.2.

Consequently, latent codes are sampled either directly from the prior p⁡(𝒛)p(\bm{z}) or through the diffusion process. In both cases, greedy autoregressive decoding maps each latent code to a grammar-admissible HGR rule sequence, after which deterministic reverse derivation reconstructs the corresponding combinatorial complex and associated molecular graph. The resulting molecules preserve the hierarchical and higher-order topology encoded by HGR strings.

HGR-based foundation model (HGR-FM)

HGR-FM (Fig. 5a) takes the HGR string 𝒓\bm{r} of a molecule as input and maps its rule tokens to initialised embeddings. The resulting token embeddings are encoded by a Grammar Transformer whose self-attention uses the higher-order position bias defined below. Contextualised atom-level token states feed atom-level pretext tasks, whereas the final hidden state of the molecule-level token serves as a fixed-length molecular fingerprint for higher-level tasks and downstream transfer.

Higher-order position encoding.

Transformers do not explicitly exploit input structure by default [57], whereas appropriate structural inductive biases can improve their performance [58, 59]. To capture the hierarchical geometry together with pairwise connectivity, we introduce a composite structural encoding into self-attention. For each attention head, the pre-softmax attention logit between tokens ii and jj takes the form

Logiti,j=(ℛ⁡(rk⁡(σi))​𝒒i)⊤​(ℛ⁡(rk⁡(σj))​𝒌j)/dh+b𝒞​(δi​j𝒞)+bρ​(ρi​j𝒞)⏟Higher-order structural encoding+𝕀i,j∈𝒢​(ϕ⁡(δi​j𝒢)+ψi​j)⏟Pairwise structural encoding.\text{Logit}_{i,j}=\underbrace{\bigl(\mathcal{R}(\operatorname{rk}(\sigma_{i}))\bm{q}_{i}\bigr)^{\top}\bigl(\mathcal{R}(\operatorname{rk}(\sigma_{j}))\bm{k}_{j}\bigr)/\sqrt{d_{h}}+b_{\mathcal{C}}(\delta^{\mathcal{C}}_{ij})+b_{\rho}(\rho^{\mathcal{C}}_{ij})}_{\text{Higher-order structural encoding}}+\underbrace{\mathbb{I}_{i,j\in\mathcal{G}}\left(\phi(\delta^{\mathcal{G}}_{ij})+\psi_{ij}\right)}_{\text{Pairwise structural encoding}}. (9)

Here, dhd_{h} is the per-head dimension, σi\sigma_{i} denotes the cell associated with token ii, and ℛ⁡(⋅)\mathcal{R}(\cdot) denotes Rotary Positional Embedding (RoPE) [60] applied to the query 𝒒i\bm{q}_{i} and key 𝒌j\bm{k}_{j} using their cell ranks. The resulting inner product encodes their relative rank difference. The learnable scalar biases b𝒞b_{\mathcal{C}} and bρb_{\rho} are shared across all layers and are indexed by the grammar-tree distance δi​j𝒞\delta^{\mathcal{C}}_{ij} and relation type ρi​j𝒞\rho^{\mathcal{C}}_{ij}, respectively. The relation types comprise self, parent, child, sibling, ancestor, descendant and other. The pair (rk⁡(σi),δi​j𝒞)(\operatorname{rk}(\sigma_{i}),\delta^{\mathcal{C}}_{ij}) forms a lossless signature of hierarchical structure for molecular complexes 𝒞\mathcal{C}, enabling precise discrimination of topological relations such as siblings and cousins.

We also add pairwise structural biases using shortest-path spatial encoding and edge-path encoding [58]. Pairwise spatial encoding is implemented as a learnable bias ϕ⁡(δi​j𝒢)\phi(\delta^{\mathcal{G}}_{ij}), indexed by the shortest-path distance δi​j𝒢\delta^{\mathcal{G}}_{ij} on the molecular graph 𝒢\mathcal{G}. Edge-path encoding ψi​j\psi_{ij} is defined as the average of edge features aggregated along the shortest path SPi​j\text{SP}_{ij}

ψi​j=1|SPi​j|​∑e∈SPi​j𝒙e⊤​𝒘posi​j​(e)ℰ,\psi_{ij}=\frac{1}{|\text{SP}_{ij}|}\sum_{e\in\mathrm{SP}_{ij}}\bm{x}_{e}^{\top}\bm{w}^{\mathcal{E}}_{\text{pos}_{ij}(e)}, (10)

where SPi​j\text{SP}_{ij} denotes edge sequence on the shortest path from ii to jj, posi​j​(e)\text{pos}_{ij}(e) indicates the relative position of edge ee along this path, 𝒙e\bm{x}_{e} is the feature of edge ee, and 𝒘nℰ\bm{w}^{\mathcal{E}}_{n} is a learnable embedding for path position nn. Pairwise biases are applied only to atom-token pairs, and are set to zero otherwise. Attention heads are partitioned across the additive encodings, so each head receives the content score together with a subset of these terms (Sec. 1.6). Together, these terms inject hierarchical cues and pairwise connectivity into attention while ensuring perturbation invariance.

Multi-level pretext tasks.

HGR-FM is pretrained with four complementary pretext tasks spanning atom-, fragment-, molecular- and 3D-conformation-level supervision [50]. The atom-level task masks atom-level rule tokens and predicts their atomic attributes from contextualised token representations, encouraging fine-grained local chemical perception. The fragment-level task predicts 1,024-bit Morgan [12] (radius 2) and 166-bit Molecular ACCess System (MACCS) [61] binary fingerprints that represent the presence or absence of specific functional groups or substructures, thereby encoding chemically meaningful local motifs. The molecular-level task regresses molecular descriptors (e.g., molecular weight, logP), encouraging the model to internalize global physicochemical properties. Finally, the 3D-level task predicts pairwise interatomic distances derived from optimised molecular conformers, enabling integration of spatial geometry. These tasks are jointly optimised using the same task weights as MORE [50]. Together, the four tasks yield transferable representations spanning local, substructural, global-property and geometric information (see Sec. 1.6 for details).

Datasets and benchmarks

RingDiv benchmark construction.

We constructed RingDiv, a ring-enriched, topology-balanced benchmark comprising 1.18 million molecules, together with a curated subset, RingDiv300k, for rapid development and ablation studies. The ring-topology coverage of both datasets is characterised in Fig. 3. It was designed to broaden coverage of complex ring architectures while retaining balanced distributions of ring size and fusion topology in drug-like chemical space. The source pool contained approximately 143 million compounds from PubChem [62], SureChEMBL [63], and five commercial screening libraries (eMolecules, Asinex, ChemDiv, Enamine and MolPort). After merging, molecules were standardised as RDKit molecular objects; unparsable entries were discarded, and repeated source records were collapsed using InChI identifiers [64] generated from the standardised structures. For each molecule, we performed ring perception and annotated ring-size and fusion-topology descriptors: ring sizes were binned as small (3–4 atoms), normal (5–7 atoms), medium (8–11 atoms), or macro (≥\geq 12 atoms), and ring systems were categorised by connectivity pattern (spirocyclic, fused, condensed, or bridged).

We then constrained the chemical space to a drug-like regime by retaining compounds with 1–10 rings and molecular weights of 100–900 Da, and excluding molecules containing macrocycles. Macrocycles are sparsely represented in the source databases and differ markedly from smaller ring systems in flexibility, synthetic accessibility, and physicochemical properties; their inclusion would introduce poorly supported outliers. These per-molecule descriptors were used to guide topology-balanced sampling and to summarise ring-topology coverage in the final benchmark.

To ensure adequate representation of structurally informative but underrepresented motifs, we adopted a two-stage sampling strategy that combines topology balancing with fingerprint-based diversity selection. First, a quota-first pass prioritised rare classes such as medium rings, spirocyclic and bridged architectures: molecules were sampled to satisfy minimum quotas for these classes, after which the remaining pool was randomly expanded into an oversampled candidate set while preserving the desired marginal topology balance. Second, to maximise structural diversity and reduce near-duplicates, candidates were encoded using 2,048-bit Morgan [12] fingerprints (radius 2), and a MaxMin diversity criterion was applied using Tanimoto similarity. This step favours subsets that are globally well dispersed in fingerprint space while discouraging highly similar neighbours, using an approximate Tanimoto-similarity threshold of 0.65 without compromising the intended ring-topology coverage. RingDiv300k was obtained from RingDiv by topology-balanced subset selection, using tighter quotas for rare ring categories rather than random subsampling.

Datasets for generation and transfer.

We evaluated de novo molecular generation on five benchmarks: QM9 [65], ZINC250k [39], MOSES [66], GuacaMol [67] and RingDiv300k. The final two benchmarks were used for the main large-scale comparisons. For foundation-model pretraining, we used three corpora: ZINC2m [39], RingDiv and their combination (ZINC2m+RingDiv). ZINC2m was the primary setting used for baseline alignment, whereas RingDiv and the combined corpus were used to assess the effect of pretraining data. Downstream transfer was evaluated on seven MoleculeNet classification benchmarks [52]: BBBP, Tox21, ToxCast, SIDER, ClinTox, HIV and BACE, each split by scaffold into 80/10/10 training, validation and test partitions [50].

Experimental setup

Generation baselines and metrics.

Generation baselines span sequence-, motif-, graph- and topology-aware molecular generators. For the main-text comparison on GuacaMol and RingDiv300k, we use the recent diffusion and higher-order-aware baselines DiGress [42], HoG-Diff [23], DeFoG [43] and SELFIES-VAE [14]. Sec. 4.2 adds dataset-specific baselines where evaluated, including MiCaM [68], MoFlow [69], EDP-GNN [70], GraphEBM [71], GDSS [72], SMILES-VAE and MHG-VAE [31]. The sequence VAE controls are reported on GuacaMol and RingDiv300k, the two main larger-scale benchmarks, whereas MHG-VAE is reported on QM9 and ZINC250k because MHG induction scales poorly to larger collections. HGR-VAE and HGR-LDF use the RSG-induced grammar unless otherwise stated. Baselines used released checkpoints or published hyperparameters where available; for new settings such as RingDiv300k, methods were re-tuned within method-specific search spaces.

Generated molecules are assessed along three axes: basic metrics (validity, uniqueness and novelty); chemistry-based distributional metrics, including Fréchet ChemNet Distance (FCD), KL score and physicochemical-property agreement; and topology-based metrics covering graph-kernel similarity, nearest-neighbour similarity, scaffold distributions and curvature-filtration descriptors [73]. These curvature-filtration descriptors are reported as auxiliary distributional checks because of their high estimation variance (Sec. 3.1). All metrics except validity are computed over valid generated molecules relative to a held-out test set. Additional metrics, full definitions and implementation details are provided in Sec. 3.1. Metric computation was also optimised to reduce evaluation overhead; representative speed-ups are shown in Fig. 5.

Foundation-model baselines and transfer protocols.

For downstream transfer, we used two protocols. Full fine-tuning jointly optimised the pretrained encoder and task-specific head. Probing froze the encoder and trained only lightweight task-specific heads, isolating representation quality while limiting overfitting on small downstream tasks. Fingerprints from the frozen encoder were cached and reused across probing runs. Baselines included representative molecular graph pretraining methods: Infomax [74], EdgePred [75], AttrMasking and ContextPred [76], GraphCL [77], GraphLoG [78], GraphMAE [79], GraphMVP [80] and MORE [50]. Transfer performance was measured using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), following the MoleculeNet convention.

Implementation details.

Generation models (HGR-VAE, HGR-LDF) and HGR-FM were implemented in PyTorch. Complete model configurations, optimisers and training hyperparameters are listed in Sec. 3.4. Unless otherwise stated, results are computed over three random seeds. Error bars in Fig. 4 denote the standard deviation across seeds. For the foundation-model transfer experiments, Fig. 5 reports the mean across seeds, and per-task standard deviations are provided in Tab. 12.

Data availability

RingDiv, RingDiv300k and other supporting data generated in this study will be publicly released upon publication. Public benchmark datasets used in this study are available from their original sources.

The code used in this study is available through the HGR GitHub repository.
