Supplementary Information

1 Model and algorithm details

1.1 Notation and terminology

We begin by summarising the key concepts and notation used in this paper.

We use the following grammar-operation terminology throughout the Supplementary Information. Let 𝒟\mathcal{D} denote the collection of input data. Induction constructs a higher-order grammar Γ\Gamma from 𝒟\mathcal{D}. A rewriting or rule-application step, written A⇒BA\Rightarrow B, replaces one non-terminal site in AA with the right-hand side of an applicable production rule, yielding BB. We write A⇒∗BA\Rightarrow^{*}B when BB is obtained from AA by a finite sequence of such rule applications; this process is called a derivation. In HGR, derivation proceeds in the generative direction. An HGR string 𝒓(m)\bm{r}^{(m)} is stored in post-order, so reconstruction from SS consumes rev⁡(𝒓(m))\operatorname{rev}(\bm{r}^{(m)}). We use S⇒𝒓(m)(𝒞m,𝒢m)S\Rightarrow^{\bm{r}^{(m)}}(\mathcal{C}_{m},\mathcal{G}_{m}) as shorthand for the derivation represented by 𝒓(m)\bm{r}^{(m)}. For a target lifted complex and associated molecular graph (𝒞,𝒢)∈𝒟(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{G})\in\mathcal{D}, parsing is the inverse task of finding an HGR string 𝒓\bm{r} such that S⇒𝒓(𝒞,𝒢)S\Rightarrow^{\bm{r}}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{G}).

1.2 Lifting algorithms

The MIG lifting procedure, summarised in Methods and detailed in Supplementary Algorithm 1, performs hierarchical subgraph merging with anchor resolution. The algorithm initialises singleton atom cells and a current partition over the molecular graph 𝒢\mathcal{G}. At each round, it scores adjacent pairs of current partition blocks by frequency, commits a maximal non-overlapping set of highest-scoring merges, and appends the resulting merged cells to the merge history ℋ\mathcal{H}. The lifted complex 𝒞MIG\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{MIG}} is formed as (𝒱,cells⁡(ℋ),rkMIG)(\mathcal{V},\operatorname{cells}(\mathcal{H}),\operatorname{rk}_{\mathrm{MIG}}), where cells⁡(ℋ)\operatorname{cells}(\mathcal{H}) collects the cells recorded in ℋ\mathcal{H}, with ranks given by cell height above the atom leaves; 𝒢\mathcal{G} supplies adjacency for candidate generation and anchor resolution. If the call to ResolveAmbiguity is omitted, Supplementary Algorithm 1 reduces to the shared frequency-guided merging step. With this subroutine, it becomes the MIG lifting variant: whenever a candidate merged cell has more than two anchors, the procedure grows the cell by best-first absorption of neighbouring partition blocks until the anchor interface has at most two anchors. The RSG variant uses the same primitives, but stages admissible merges around ring systems (Methods), so we do not repeat its pseudocode.

1.3 Grammar induction

Grammar induction constructs a shared HGR corpus by parsing lifted complexes and their associated molecular graphs into HGR strings. Here we describe the contraction hierarchy, parsing algorithm, library-level rule induction, reverse derivation and reconstruction guarantees. In this construction, 𝒞\mathcal{C} supplies the lifted cell hierarchy, whereas 𝒢\mathcal{G} supplies the pairwise bonds and anchor interfaces required for rule construction. For the cell families produced by our lifting algorithms, any two cells are either disjoint or nested, so set inclusion defines a contraction tree. Singleton atom cells are leaves, and a larger cell is the parent of a contained cell when no intermediate cell exists between them in 𝒳\mathcal{X}. The rank rk⁡(σ)\operatorname{rk}(\sigma) measures the height of σ\sigma above the atom leaves and is defined as the maximum number of edges from σ\sigma to an atom leaf. It is therefore determined by 𝒳\mathcal{X}. We serialise all cells, including singleton atom cells, in post-order. We call a serialisation admissible when each child subtree forms a contiguous block before its parent; sibling subtrees may occur in any order. Different admissible serializations may produce alternative HGR strings for the same lifted complex. Each string remains lossless under the corresponding reverse derivation and may serve as optional data augmentation.

Parsing and rule induction.

The parsing procedure for a single lifted complex is summarised in Supplementary Algorithm 2. For the current working graph 𝒢~\widetilde{\mathcal{G}} and a vertex set UU, 𝒢~​[U]\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}[U] denotes the subgraph induced by UU. The hatted graphs 𝒢^kL\widehat{\mathcal{G}}^{L}_{k} and 𝒢^kR\widehat{\mathcal{G}}^{R}_{k} are the candidate left- and right-hand sides constructed at parsing step kk. LookupOrInsert maps this pair to a compatible corpus rule rik:𝒢ikL→𝒢ikRr_{i_{k}}:\mathcal{G}^{L}_{i_{k}}\to\mathcal{G}^{R}_{i_{k}}, inserting the candidate if necessary, and returns its index iki_{k}. Compatibility requires structural isomorphism that respects the ordered anchor interface and child-site correspondence. Across a molecule library, ParseComplex is applied to each lifted complex and its associated molecular graph.

After all complexes have been parsed, the shared corpus 𝒫\mathcal{P} defines the grammar Γ=(Σ,𝒩,S,𝒫)\Gamma=(\Sigma,\mathcal{N},S,\mathcal{P}). Each molecule is assigned an HGR string 𝒓(m)\bm{r}^{(m)}, whose rule tokens refer to rules in 𝒫\mathcal{P}. Multiple cell occurrences can therefore contribute tokens that refer to the same production rule. Anchor resolution during lifting further reduces rule fragmentation. Corpus growth and rule reuse are quantified on ZINC250k (Fig. 2b,c) and QM9 (Fig. 4). Each HGR string and its referenced rules define a lossless inverse process.

Reverse derivation and exact reconstruction.

Given an HGR string 𝒓=[ri1,…,riL]\bm{r}=[r_{i_{1}},\dots,r_{i_{L}}], reverse derivation starts from SS and consumes rev⁡(𝒓)=[riL,…,ri1]\operatorname{rev}(\bm{r})=[r_{i_{L}},\dots,r_{i_{1}}]. The decoder maintains a LIFO stack of pending non-terminal sites, initialised as [S][S]. At reverse step k=L,…,1k=L,\dots,1, it pops the next site and applies the corpus rule rikr_{i_{k}}. The ordered anchor interface reconnects boundary bonds, after which child non-terminal sites are pushed in reverse of their stored order. Decoding succeeds only if the stack is empty after ri1r_{i_{1}} has been applied.

Exact reconstruction relies on the ordered rule sequence and, within each rule, the right-hand-side graph with its ordered child non-terminal sites and the ordered anchor interface. Together, these records specify the derivation tree, cell hierarchy and boundary correspondence. The rank function need not be stored separately because it is recovered as cell height in the contraction tree. For this guarantee, the reconstructed object is the pair (𝒞,𝒢)(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{G}), where 𝒞\mathcal{C} is the lifted complex and 𝒢\mathcal{G} is the associated molecular graph. For an admissible serialisation τ\tau, let ParseΓ,τ⁡(𝒞,𝒢)\operatorname{Parse}_{\Gamma,\tau}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{G}) denote the HGR string returned by ParseComplex. Let DerΓ⁡(𝒓)\operatorname{Der}_{\Gamma}(\bm{r}) denote the pair produced by reverse derivation. For claims on isomorphism classes, atom order is fixed by the same canonical molecular labelling used for serialisation; otherwise the statement is read for labelled complexes.

Proposition 1 (Exact reconstruction).

Let η∈{MIG,RSG}\eta\in\{\mathrm{MIG},\mathrm{RSG}\} denote either lifting variant. For any admissible serialisation τ\tau, reverse derivation exactly recovers any lifted complex 𝒞η\mathcal{C}_{\eta} and its associated molecular graph 𝒢\mathcal{G} after parsing by ParseComplex,

DerΓ⁡(ParseΓ,τ⁡(𝒞η,𝒢))=(𝒞η,𝒢).\operatorname{Der}_{\Gamma}\!\left(\operatorname{Parse}_{\Gamma,\tau}(\mathcal{C}_{\eta},\mathcal{G})\right)=(\mathcal{C}_{\eta},\mathcal{G}).
Proof.

At parsing step kk, ParseComplex appends the rule token rikr_{i_{k}} and replaces σ~k\widetilde{\sigma}_{k} with a fresh non-terminal site Nk∗N_{k}^{*}. Let (𝒞(k),𝒢(k))(\mathcal{C}^{(k)},\mathcal{G}^{(k)}) represent the intermediate parsing state after this contraction. Initially, (𝒞(0),𝒢(0))=(𝒞,𝒢)(\mathcal{C}^{(0)},\mathcal{G}^{(0)})=(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{G}), whereas the final state (𝒞(L),𝒢(L))(\mathcal{C}^{(L)},\mathcal{G}^{(L)}) is represented by SS. Let (𝒞^(k),𝒢^(k))(\widehat{\mathcal{C}}^{(k)},\widehat{\mathcal{G}}^{(k)}) denote the decoder state after applying riL,…,rik+1r_{i_{L}},\dots,r_{i_{k+1}} in reverse derivation.

The ordered rule tokens and child non-terminal sites determine the derivation tree, while the ordered anchor interfaces fix the boundary correspondences. If the parsing and decoder states agree after step kk, applying rikr_{i_{k}} restores exactly the cell representation, child sites, and bonds removed by the kkth contraction. Therefore,

(𝒞^(k),𝒢^(k))=(𝒞(k),𝒢(k))⟹(𝒞^(k−1),𝒢^(k−1))=(𝒞(k−1),𝒢(k−1)).(\widehat{\mathcal{C}}^{(k)},\widehat{\mathcal{G}}^{(k)})=(\mathcal{C}^{(k)},\mathcal{G}^{(k)})\Longrightarrow(\widehat{\mathcal{C}}^{(k-1)},\widehat{\mathcal{G}}^{(k-1)})=(\mathcal{C}^{(k-1)},\mathcal{G}^{(k-1)}).

The final parsing state and initial decoder state at k=Lk=L are both represented by SS, establishing the induction base. Downward induction over k=L,…,1k=L,\dots,1 therefore restores the cell-inclusion hierarchy and the associated molecular graph. Because rk⁡(σ)\operatorname{rk}(\sigma) is defined as the height of σ\sigma in the contraction tree, the restored tree uniquely determines rk\operatorname{rk}. Hence, (𝒞^(0),𝒢^(0))=(𝒞,𝒢)(\widehat{\mathcal{C}}^{(0)},\widehat{\mathcal{G}}^{(0)})=(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{G}), completing the reconstruction. ∎

Grammar-constrained generation and validity.

For generation, the reverse-derivation decoder predicts rules in the order corresponding to rev⁡(𝒓)\operatorname{rev}(\bm{r}), beginning with the root rule. At each step, the stack top selects the pending non-terminal site to expand. The admissibility mask retains only rules whose left-hand-side ordered anchor interface matches the interface at that site. After expansion, newly introduced child non-terminal sites are pushed onto the stack. Reversing the completed output recovers the post-order HGR string. A sequence is accepted only when all selected rules have been applied and the stack is empty. Every cell and bond in the resulting object then comes from an applied rule, while cell ranks follow from the completed derivation tree. This establishes grammar-level completion; the chemical scope of “valid by construction” requires the rule-origin condition stated next.

Suppose that every applied rule was induced from a valence-consistent molecular graph. Each rule records its right-hand-side graph, bond attributes and ordered anchor interface. Derivation therefore introduces only atoms, bonds and local attachment patterns recorded by these rules. Restricting rule application to a matching ordered anchor interface preserves the local valence and bonding constraints encoded by the grammar. Under these conditions, every completed derivation is grammar-valid by construction. This guarantee does not extend to properties absent from the grammar, including stereochemical realizability and synthesizability, which remain empirical outcomes.

1.4 Structure-aware rule initialisation

In the generation model, each rule token is initialised from a combination of Weisfeiler–Lehman (WL) structure-aware features and a learned per-rule embedding. For the molecular foundation model, we use a fully structure-derived initialisation that combines these WL features with a complementary Random Walk Positional Encoding (RWPE).

Weisfeiler–Lehman histogram embedding.

For each production rule ri∈𝒫r_{i}\in\mathcal{P}, we construct a fixed-length, order-invariant feature vector by aggregating WL labels over its right-hand-side graph 𝒢iR=(Vi,Ei)\mathcal{G}^{R}_{i}=(V_{i},E_{i}). The WL refinement proceeds for HH iterations.

At the initialisation step (t=0t=0), each node is assigned a canonical attribute label derived from stable atomic properties (e.g., symbol, aromaticity, degree, ring membership) and structural markers (e.g., anchor flags). These tokens are lexicographically sorted and concatenated to ensure permutation invariance. In subsequent rounds (t=1,…,H−1)(t=1,\dots,H-1), node labels are iteratively refined by concatenating each node’s previous label with the sorted multiset of its neighbours’ labels, following the standard 1-WL refinement scheme.

We define a label universe Λ(t)={λ1(t),…,λ|Λ(t)|(t)}\Lambda^{(t)}=\{\lambda^{(t)}_{1},\dots,\lambda^{(t)}_{|\Lambda^{(t)}|}\} for each iteration tt, which contains all distinct WL labels observed across rules and an ⟨UNK⟩\langle\text{UNK}\rangle to handle unseen structures during inference. Each rule rir_{i} is then represented by a normalised histogram of label occurrences:

hi,j(t)=1|Vi|∑v∈Vi𝟙{ℓv(t)=λj(t)},j=1,…,|Λ(t)|,h_{i,j}^{(t)}=\frac{1}{|V_{i}|}\sum_{v\in V_{i}}\mathds{1}\bigl\{\ell_{v}^{(t)}=\lambda_{j}^{(t)}\bigr\},\quad j=1,\dots,|\Lambda^{(t)}|,

where ℓv(t)\ell_{v}^{(t)} denotes the WL label assigned to node vv in rule rir_{i} at refinement round tt, and 𝟙​{⋅}\mathds{1}\{\cdot\} is the indicator function. Stacking all hi(t)h_{i}^{(t)} across rules yields a sparse matrix 𝐒(t)∈ℝ|𝒫|×|Λt|\mathbf{S}^{(t)}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{P}|\times|\Lambda_{t}|}, whose ii-th row corresponds to the histogram of rule rir_{i}.

The cumulative WL feature for rule rir_{i} is obtained by concatenating the histograms from all refinement rounds:

𝐳iWL=[𝐒i(0)∥𝐒i(1)∥…∥𝐒i(H−1)],\mathbf{z}_{i}^{\mathrm{WL}}=\bigl[\mathbf{S}_{i}^{(0)}\mathbin{\|}\mathbf{S}_{i}^{(1)}\mathbin{\|}\dots\mathbin{\|}\mathbf{S}_{i}^{(H-1)}\bigr],

where 𝐒i(t)\mathbf{S}_{i}^{(t)} denotes the ii-th row of 𝐒(t)\mathbf{S}^{(t)}. This embedding is invariant to node and neighbourhood ordering, supports sparse storage and large-scale GPU computation, and extends to previously unseen rules. In our grammars, WL embedding already yields distinct initial features for more than 98%98\% of production rules, indicating strong identifiability.

Random walk-based rule features.

To further increase the discriminative power of rule initialisation beyond the WL histogram, we augment each production rule with a random walk positional encoding (RWPE) [81, 82] computed on the rule’s right-hand side graph.

For each rule rir_{i}, we first extract its adjacency matrix A∈ℝ|Vi|×|Vi|A\in\mathbb{R}^{|V_{i}|\times|V_{i}|} based on its RHS graph 𝒢iR=(Vi,Ei)\mathcal{G}^{R}_{i}=(V_{i},E_{i}). We then construct a random walk transition matrix

P=D−1​A,Di​i=∑jAi​j,P=D^{-1}A,\quad D_{ii}=\sum_{j}A_{ij},

where DD is the degree matrix. The structural signature of a node vv is defined as the vector of return probabilities over KK steps:

𝐩v=[(P)v​v,(P2)v​v,…,(PK)v​v]∈ℝK.\mathbf{p}_{v}=\big[(P)_{vv},(P^{2})_{vv},\ldots,(P^{K})_{vv}\big]\in\mathbb{R}^{K}.

We compute these values iteratively via Pt+1=Pt​PP^{t+1}=P^{t}P and assemble them into a node feature matrix 𝐑∈ℝn×K\mathbf{R}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times K}, where the vv-th row corresponds to 𝐩v\mathbf{p}_{v}.

To ensure invariance to node permutation, we impose a canonical ordering on the nodes by performing a lexicographical sort on the rows of 𝐑\mathbf{R}. To map graphs of varying sizes to a fixed-dimensional space, we truncate or pad the sorted matrix to a maximum size NmaxN_{\max}. The processed matrix is then flattened to form the rule-level RWPE vector:

𝐳iRW=vec⁡(PadOrTrunc⁡(LexSort⁡(𝐑),Nmax))∈ℝNmax​K.\mathbf{z}_{i}^{\mathrm{RW}}=\mathrm{vec}\Bigl(\mathrm{PadOrTrunc}\bigl(\mathrm{LexSort}(\mathbf{R});N_{\max}\bigr)\Bigr)\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{\max}K}.

This encoding relies solely on graph topology, providing a complementary signal to the attribute-based WL features. The final initialised embedding 𝐳i\mathbf{z}_{i} for rule rir_{i} is the concatenation of both components:

𝐳i=[𝐳iWL∥𝐳iRW].\mathbf{z}_{i}=\bigl[\mathbf{z}_{i}^{\mathrm{WL}}\mathbin{\|}\mathbf{z}_{i}^{\mathrm{RW}}\bigr].

The inclusion of 𝐳iRW\mathbf{z}_{i}^{\mathrm{RW}} provides an additional topological signal that can distinguish structurally distinct rules with identical WL colourings.

1.5 HGR-based de novo generation

1.5.1 Grammar variational autoencoder

The HGR generative model is a sequence-to-sequence grammar variational autoencoder (GVAE) that operates on HGR strings rather than atoms (Fig. 2).

For all reported HGR-VAE and HGR-LDF results, each rule token is mapped to a WL-structured embedding, and a Transformer encoder maps the resulting variable-length sequence to a fixed-dimensional summary. This representation parameterises the Gaussian posterior qϕ​(𝒛∣𝒓)q_{\bm{\phi}}(\bm{z}\mid\bm{r}), from which a latent code 𝒛∈ℝd\bm{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is sampled using the reparameterization trick.

The decoder is a 𝒛\bm{z}-conditioned GRU that autoregressively generates production rules, with grammar constraints applied at each decoding step. A last-in-first-out stack determines which pending non-terminal site is expanded next, while anchor-interface matching restricts rule selection to admissible production rules. During decoding, rule generation is capped at the dataset-specific maximum sequence length. Sequences whose stacks remain non-empty at this limit are discarded as incomplete derivations; completed HGR strings are syntactically valid and decode deterministically to molecular complexes. The model is trained with the β\beta-VAE objective defined in Methods under a cyclical Kullback–Leibler annealing schedule. The network widths, depths and per-dataset training settings are listed in Tab. 4.

1.5.2 Latent diffusion sampling

To further improve sample quality, we model the GVAE latent space with a score-based diffusion framework that perturbs latent codes with noise and trains a neural network to reverse this corruption. Sampling then starts from a tractable prior and follows the learned reverse process to generate latent codes approximating the target distribution p⁡(𝒛0)p(\bm{z}_{0}) [54, 55].

Specifically, the time-dependent forward process of the diffusion model can be described by the following stochastic differential equation (SDE):

d​𝒛t=𝒇t​(𝒛t)​d​t+gt​d​𝒘t,\mathrm{d}\bm{z}_{t}=\bm{f}_{t}\left(\bm{z}_{t}\right)\mathrm{d}t+g_{t}\mathrm{d}\bm{w}_{t},

where 𝒇t:ℝn→ℝn\bm{f}_{t}:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{n} is a vector-valued drift function, gt:[0,T]→ℝg_{t}:[0,T]\to\mathbb{R} is a scalar diffusion coefficient, and 𝒘t\bm{w}_{t} represents a Wiener process. Under this SDE, p⁡(𝒛0)p(\bm{z}_{0}) evolves to p⁡(𝒛T)p(\bm{z}_{T}), which for sufficiently large TT approximates a tractable prior, such as a standard Gaussian distribution.

Starting from time TT, p⁡(𝒛T)p(\bm{z}_{T}) can be progressively transformed back to p⁡(𝒛0)p(\bm{z}_{0}) by following the trajectory of the reverse-time SDE [83],

d​𝒛t=[𝒇t​(𝒛t)−gt2​∇𝒛t​log​pt​(𝒛t)⏟score function]​⁡d​t¯+gt​d​𝒘¯t,\mathrm{d}\bm{z}_{t}=[\bm{f}_{t}(\bm{z}_{t})-g_{t}^{2}\underbrace{\nabla_{\bm{z}_{t}}\log p_{t}(\bm{z}_{t})}_{\text{score function}}]\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}{\bar{t}}+g_{t}\mathrm{d}\bar{\bm{w}}_{t},

where pt​(⋅)p_{t}(\cdot) denotes the probability density function of 𝒛t\bm{z}_{t} and 𝒘¯\bar{\bm{w}} is a reverse-time Wiener process.

The term ∇𝒛t​log​pt​(𝒛t)\nabla_{\bm{z}_{t}}\log p_{t}(\bm{z}_{t}), known as the score function, is typically parameterised by a neural network 𝒔𝜽​(𝒛t,t)\bm{s}_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{z}_{t},t) and trained using the conditional score-matching loss function [56]:

ℓ⁡(𝜽)≜𝔼t,𝒛t​[ω⁡(t)​‖𝒔𝜽​(𝒛t,t)−∇𝒛t​log​pt​(𝒛t)‖2]∝𝔼t,𝒛0,𝒛t​[ω⁡(t)​‖𝒔𝜽​(𝒛t,t)−∇𝒛t​log​pt​(𝒛t|𝒛0)‖2],\ell(\bm{\theta})\triangleq\mathbb{E}_{t,\bm{z}_{t}}\left[\omega(t)\left\|\bm{s}_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{z}_{t},t)-\nabla_{\bm{z}_{t}}\log p_{t}(\bm{z}_{t})\right\|^{2}\right]\propto\mathbb{E}_{t,\bm{z}_{0},\bm{z}_{t}}\left[\omega(t)\left\|\bm{s}_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{z}_{t},t)-\nabla_{\bm{z}_{t}}\log p_{t}(\bm{z}_{t}|\bm{z}_{0})\right\|^{2}\right],

where ω⁡(t)\omega(t) is a weighting function. The second form is more commonly used because the conditional probability pt​(𝒛t|𝒛0)p_{t}(\bm{z}_{t}|\bm{z}_{0}) is tractable. Generation then samples 𝒛T\bm{z}_{T} from a tractable prior p⁡(𝒛T)≈pprior​(𝒛)p(\bm{z}_{T})\approx p_{\mathrm{prior}}(\bm{z}) and recovers 𝒛0\bm{z}_{0} by numerically solving the reverse-time SDE.

In HGR-LDF the score network 𝒔𝜽\bm{s}_{\bm{\theta}} is a latent diffusion Transformer that operates on the standardised GVAE posterior means while the grammar decoder is left unchanged; its architecture, the variance-preserving noise schedule and the predictor sampler are specified in Tab. 5.

1.6 HGR-FM architecture and pretraining

HGR-FM operates on HGR strings and is pretrained on large molecular datasets. It combines structure-aware rule embeddings with a Grammar Transformer backbone, a higher-order position encoding and a multi-level pretext objective.

Grammar Transformer backbone.

The Grammar Transformer is the shared encoder backbone of HGR-FM. Each rule token is mapped to a structure-aware embedding (Sec. 1.4) and linearly projected to the model width, with dedicated vectors for padding and special boundary tokens. A stack of Transformer layers then processes the sequence. After the final layer, contextualized atom-level token embeddings feed atom-level tasks, whereas the final hidden state of the molecule-level token serves as a fixed-length molecular fingerprint for fragment-, molecule- and 3D-level tasks and downstream transfer.

Higher-order position encoding.

Within each Transformer layer, self-attention is augmented with a composite higher-order bias, defined in Methods. This bias combines rank-aware rotary position encoding over cell height, additive biases indexed by grammar-tree distance and discrete relation type, and shortest-path spatial and edge-path biases [58] on atom-token pairs. Attention heads are divided into four equal groups. Rank-aware RoPE is applied to all heads; one group receives no additive structural bias, whereas the other three receive the grammar-tree, shortest-path and edge-path biases, respectively. Per-layer learnable scales weight the three additive biases.

Pretext tasks.

Supervised molecular labels are often task-specific and costly to obtain, whereas large unlabelled molecular libraries are readily available. HGR-FM therefore uses multi-level pretext objectives to learn transferable representations from unlabelled molecules. Following the multi-level objective design of MORE [50], these tasks cover atom masking, substructure-fingerprint prediction, descriptor regression and conformation-distance prediction. They provide atom-, fragment-, molecule- and 3D-conformation-level supervision, respectively. The atom- and fragment-level tasks are adapted to the HGR rule-token input.

Atom-level task. During data collation, 25% of atoms are sampled for masking, with at least one masked atom per molecule. The atom feature is replaced by a mask token and, when grammar inputs are used, the corresponding rule-sequence position is replaced by the grammar mask token. The target is the original atom type over the atom vocabulary. A one-layer GIN decoder reconstructs this target from contextualized atom-token embeddings using the scaled cosine-error loss [79]. This task supervises local atomic environments.

Fragment-level task. For fragment-level supervision, the model predicts two binary substructure targets: 1,024-bit Morgan fingerprints (radius 2) [12] and 166-bit Molecular ACCess System (MACCS) [61] fingerprints. These targets expose functional-group and local-substructure information not captured by atom masking alone.

Molecular-level task. For molecular-level supervision, the target vector contains standardised RDKit descriptors, including molecular weight and logP, to represent global physicochemical properties.

3D-conformation-level task. For 3D-conformation supervision, optimised conformers provide pairwise interatomic-distance targets, adding geometric constraints to the HGR-string representation.

The resulting weighted pretraining loss uses the per-task coefficients λ\lambda listed in Tab. 6. Together, the tasks supervise complementary scales, from individual atoms to whole-molecule geometry.

2 RingDiv dataset construction

2.1 Source databases and curation

This section documents the construction of the RingDiv datasets: RingDiv (1.18 million molecules) and RingDiv300k, a curated development subset used for rapid experiments and ablation studies. It covers source aggregation, molecular standardisation, ring-topology annotation and quota-balanced diversity sampling.

The starting pool combined approximately 143143 million compounds from PubChem [62], SureChEMBL [63], and five commercial screening libraries: eMolecules, Asinex, ChemDiv, Enamine and MolPort. All structures were standardised and converted to RDKit molecular objects. Entries that failed RDKit parsing were removed. Source-level duplicates were removed using InChI identifiers [64] generated from the standardised structures, so repeated records from different repositories were collapsed before filtering.

Ring perception was performed on the standardised pool to obtain ring-size and fusion-topology descriptors. Ring sizes were binned as small (3–4 atoms), normal (5–7 atoms), medium (8–11 atoms) or macro (≥12\geq 12 atoms). Ring systems were also labelled by connectivity pattern as spirocyclic, fused, condensed or bridged. The annotated pool was filtered to focus on drug-like ring-containing small molecules. We retained compounds with 1–10 rings and molecular weights of 100–900 Da, and excluded molecules containing macrocycles. Macrocycles were excluded because they were sparse in the source databases and differ from common ring systems in conformational flexibility and synthetic accessibility. The resulting per-molecule descriptors were used to guide quota-balanced sampling and to quantify ring-topology coverage in the released benchmark.

2.2 Quota-balanced diversity sampling

Sampling proceeded in two stages to balance rare ring topologies with whole-molecule structural diversity. First, quotas were defined using the ring-system descriptors described above, with emphasis on relatively rare but structurally informative categories such as medium rings, spirocyclic systems and bridged systems. Molecules were drawn until the minimum quota for each rare class was met, and the remaining sampling budget was filled by random expansion into an oversampled candidate set. This step preserved the intended marginal balance across topology classes before diversity selection.

In the second stage, the oversampled candidates were encoded as 2,048-bit Morgan fingerprints (radius 2) [12]. A MaxMin criterion based on pairwise Tanimoto similarities was then used to select a globally dispersed subset while suppressing near-duplicate neighbours. We used an approximate Tanimoto-similarity threshold of 0.65, which reduced redundancy without eroding the rare-topology coverage established by the quota pass.

2.3 RingDiv variants

RingDiv is the full released benchmark produced by the curation and sampling procedure above. RingDiv300k is a smaller topology-balanced subset selected from RingDiv, using tighter quotas for rare ring categories while retaining the same drug-like scope. The two variants therefore share provenance, preprocessing and filtering criteria, but differ in scale and rare-ring balance. Dataset sizes and per-tag molecule counts are given in Tab. 2.

3 Experimental setup

3.1 Molecular generation metrics

We categorize the evaluation metrics into three groups: basic metrics, chemistry-based metrics, and topology-based metrics. This last group includes graph-level similarity, nearest-neighbour and scaffold distribution measures, and curvature-filtration descriptors based on persistent homology.

For QM9, ZINC250k, RingDiv300k and GuacaMol, we evaluated 10,000 generated molecules; for MOSES, we used 25,000 molecules, matching the benchmark protocols used by the compared methods [42]. MOSES and GuacaMol were evaluated with their official benchmarking libraries. We follow the MOSES evaluation convention [66]: validity is assessed on the raw generated set, whereas all other scores use the valid subset GG and compare it with the corresponding reference set RR. Unless noted otherwise, chemistry- and topology-based metrics quantify agreement between GG and RR; the preferred direction is marked in the result tables (Sec. 4.2).

  • •

    Validity reports the proportion of generated structures that pass molecular parsing and sanitisation, including basic valence and bonding checks.

  • •

    Uniqueness measures how many valid outputs remain after canonicalisation and duplicate removal.

  • •

    Novelty is computed after validity filtering and canonicalisation by treating any output that matches a training molecule as a repeat. Small values therefore indicate training-set recall rather than exploration of new chemical structures.

  • •

    V.U.N. combines these three criteria by counting molecules that are valid, unique and novel.

  • •

    Fréchet ChemNet Distance (FCD) embeds generated and reference molecules with ChemNet, a neural network trained on bioactivity-related molecular data [84]. Let μG,ΣG\mu_{G},\Sigma_{G} and μR,ΣR\mu_{R},\Sigma_{R} denote the empirical means and covariance matrices of the penultimate-layer ChemNet activations for GG and RR. The distance is

    FCD⁡(G,R)=‖μG−μR‖22+Tr⁡(ΣG+ΣR−2​(ΣG​ΣR)1/2).\mathrm{FCD}(G,R)=\left\|\mu_{G}-\mu_{R}\right\|_{2}^{2}+\operatorname{Tr}\left(\Sigma_{G}+\Sigma_{R}-2(\Sigma_{G}\Sigma_{R})^{1/2}\right).

    Lower FCD indicates closer distributions in this learned feature space. We use it as a primary distribution-learning metric because it summarises both location and spread. It remains a Gaussian summary of learned features, so we interpret it together with validity, novelty and structure-level metrics rather than as a standalone measure of generation quality.

  • •

    KL score follows the GuacaMol distribution-learning benchmark and compares descriptor distributions between generated and reference molecules [67]. Descriptor-wise Kullback–Leibler divergences are transformed into a bounded score. Higher values indicate better property-distribution agreement.

  • •

    Synthetic Accessibility (SA) is a heuristic estimate of synthetic difficulty [44]. When SA is reported with a downward arrow, we report a discrepancy from the reference distribution rather than the raw molecule-level score.

  • •

    Neighborhood Subgraph Pairwise Distance Kernel (NSPDK) evaluates graph-topological agreement through the MMD between generated and test-set molecules, using node and edge features.

  • •

    Similarity to a nearest neighbour (SNN) asks whether each generated molecule has a close analogue in the reference set [66]. We compute it as the average Morgan-fingerprint Tanimoto similarity between each generated molecule and its nearest reference-set neighbour. SNN is best interpreted jointly with novelty: it checks whether generated molecules stay near the reference-set chemical manifold, but by itself it cannot distinguish faithful local chemistry from nearest-neighbour memorization.

  • •

    Scaffold similarity (Scaf) reduces each molecule set to a Bemis–Murcko scaffold count vector [85]. Following the MOSES benchmark definition [66], we compare generated and reference scaffold-count vectors by cosine similarity. Scaf is complementary to SNN because it aggregates core-framework frequencies at the dataset level rather than nearest-neighbour similarity at the molecule level. It can therefore reveal whether a generator preserves the scaffold composition of the reference set, while still allowing molecule-level novelty through different substitutions or side chains.

  • •

    Filter score is reported for MOSES and gives the share of generated molecules retained by the benchmark’s medicinal-chemistry and structural filters [66].

  • •

    Curvature-filtration descriptors. We use the curvature-filtration framework [73] to compare graph topology through persistent homology of edge filtrations, complementing the substructure and graph-kernel metrics above. The framework assigns a scalar curvature to each edge under two complementary notions: Ollivier–Ricci curvature κOR\kappa_{\mathrm{OR}}, defined from the 11-Wasserstein distance between local neighbourhood distributions, and Balanced Forman curvature κBF\kappa_{\mathrm{BF}} [86], which depends on endpoint degrees and local cycle counts, including triangles and chordless 44-cycles. Each curvature induces an edge filtration of the molecular graph; we compute its 00- and 11-dimensional persistent homology, summarise each diagram as a persistence landscape and compare the landscape distributions of generated and reference sets. Because these descriptors showed high sampling variance at the evaluated sample sizes (reference-versus-reference coefficients of variation, roughly 30-60%), we report them as auxiliary distributional checks rather than primary ranking metrics.

3.2 Functional-group profiling

Following prior work on functional-group diversity [87], we used SMARTS-based substructure profiling to compare the local chemical composition of generated molecules with the RingDiv300k real test set. This analysis complements global fingerprint- and distribution-level metrics by asking whether generated molecules retain recognizable organic functional motifs spanning the categories profiled here.

Reference and generated SMILES were standardised before profiling. We canonicalised SMILES without stereochemical annotations, normalised common functional states, neutralised charged groups where possible, retained the largest fragment, and sanitised the resulting RDKit molecule. Molecules that could not be parsed or sanitised were excluded from this profiling step.

Functional groups were assigned by RDKit substructure matching with SMARTS queries adapted from ref. [87]. Each SMARTS query defined one functional-group category, such as carboxylic acid, ester, amide, ketone, aldehyde, primary or secondary amine, tertiary amine, alcohol, phenol, ether, epoxide, thiol, thioether, sulfonamide, halogen, and representative aromatic or special ring motifs. We list the exact SMARTS implementations used in this study in Fig. 3.

For each molecule, a functional group was recorded as present if at least one matching substructure was found, irrespective of the number of matches. Frequencies reported in Fig. 4a,b are therefore molecule-level occurrence rates rather than raw substructure counts. Categories are non-exclusive, so a molecule can contribute to several functional groups. For readability, the main figure separates common functional groups from less frequent or special motifs. Within each panel, chemically related groups are separated by dashed guides and ordered by their frequency in the real test set.

3.3 HGR-FM training and evaluation

We evaluated downstream transfer on seven MoleculeNet benchmarks [52], spanning biophysical, physiological and toxicity-related molecular properties. Biophysical tasks include HIV, which measures HIV replication inhibition; BACE, which measures inhibition of human β\beta-secretase 1 (BACE-1); and the Side Effect Resource (SIDER), which groups the side effects of marketed drugs into 27 system organ classes. Physiological and toxicity-related tasks include Blood-brain barrier penetration (BBBP), which predicts blood-brain barrier permeability for molecules targeting the central nervous system. Tox21, ClinTox and ToxCast focus on toxicity-related endpoints.

The baseline-aligned downstream comparison used ZINC2m pretraining, whereas separate pretraining-data analyses used RingDiv and joint ZINC2m++RingDiv pretraining. We used the standard MoleculeNet scaffold split protocol, with 80/10/10 training, validation and test partitions [50]. Compared with random splitting, scaffold splitting partitions molecules by core substructure, yielding a more challenging but more realistic evaluation of generalisation. For downstream transfer, we evaluated two protocols, full fine-tuning and frozen-encoder probing, both with early stopping on validation performance. Both protocols used the same shallow three-layer multilayer perceptron (MLP) prediction head. In full fine-tuning, the encoder and head were updated jointly; in probing, the encoder was frozen and only the head was trained. We repeated each experiment across three random seeds and report the mean and standard deviation of test performance. The same hyperparameters were used for both probing and full fine-tuning across all downstream tasks, without task-specific tuning (listed in Tab. 6).

3.4 Model configurations and training hyperparameters

The tables below summarise the principal architecture and optimisation settings, with continuous values rounded for readability. Complete per-run configurations, including dataset-specific scheduler, diffusion and optimiser settings, are provided with the code release.

The grammar variational autoencoders (Tab. 4) share a rotary-position Transformer encoder with attention pooling, a GRU decoder, hybrid structural rule initialisation, AdamW optimisation, linear warm-up, and cyclical β\beta-annealing. The MIG-grammar ablation follows the same recipe, differing only in independently searched architecture and optimisation values.

The latent diffusion samplers (Tab. 5) operate on standardised GVAE posterior means. All use a variance-preserving SDE, Euler–Maruyama sampling without a corrector, final denoising, input LayerNorm and exponential-moving-average training. Dataset-specific diffusion, architecture and optimisation settings are provided in the released configurations. Tab. 6 summarises the molecular foundation model.

4 Supplementary results and analyses

4.1 Extended grammar analysis

Grammar statistics on ZINC250k [39] form the primary analysis. Here we provide complementary results on QM9 [65] (Fig. 4), which exhibit the same qualitative trends. We restrict this cross-method comparison to these two relatively small datasets because MIG and MHG induction are substantially slower on larger corpora, and MHG yields a rapidly inflating rule corpus. The MIG-induced variant is therefore reported as a supplementary grammar-construction ablation, whereas HGR-VAE and HGR-LDF use the RSG-induced grammar unless otherwise stated.

4.2 Extended generation benchmarks

The extended tables report the basic, chemistry- and topology-based metrics defined above, including validity without correction, uniqueness, novelty, V.U.N. [72], Fréchet ChemNet Distance (FCD) [84], KL score [67], SA distribution [44], Neighborhood Subgraph Pairwise Distance Kernel (NSPDK) MMD [88], SNN, scaffold similarity and curvature-based descriptors [73]. Arrows indicate the preferred direction of each metric (↑\uparrow: higher values indicate better performance; ↓\downarrow: lower values indicate better performance). Best values for rank-interpretable metrics are shown in bold. Curvature-filtration descriptors are reported as auxiliary metrics and are not highlighted.

Additional MOSES-specific baselines include GraphINVENT [89], DisCo [90] and Cometh [91]; the remaining generation baselines are described in Methods. MHG-VAE [31] is included only for QM9 and ZINC250k, where direct comparison with a molecular hypergraph grammar baseline is feasible. We omit it from larger generation benchmarks because MHG induction is substantially slower and yields a rapidly expanding rule corpus, consistent with the grammar-analysis results.

4.3 HGR-FM transfer benchmarks

The complete task-level transfer results for the pretrained molecular encoders are reported in Tab. 12. This table complements the normalised summary in Fig. 5b by showing the original per-task AUC values and across-run standard deviations under both probing and full fine-tuning.

4.4 Computational efficiency analysis

All experiments in this work, including the runtime measurements reported below, were performed with PyTorch on a single NVIDIA L40S GPU (46 GB memory) and an AMD EPYC 9374F 32-core processor.

We analyse computational cost from two complementary perspectives: (i) evaluation-time overhead, which can dominate large-scale benchmarking when many metrics are computed across datasets and random seeds; and (ii) model-side runtime, which includes training and inference and determines practical iteration speed and sample throughput.

4.4.1 Evaluation optimisation

To improve the scalability of our evaluation pipeline, we implemented targeted optimizations for the most time-consuming metrics. As shown in Fig. 5a, the NSPDK computation is accelerated by approximately 5-fold. We also obtain substantial speedups for the curvature-filtration descriptors (κO​R\kappa_{OR} and κB​F\kappa_{BF}), with nearly 2-fold acceleration.

Fig. 5b shows that these gains are consistent across additional standard benchmarks (QM9, ZINC250k, MOSES, and GuacaMol), indicating that the optimised implementations reduce evaluation overhead across several data regimes. Overall, these optimisations increase evaluation throughput while preserving metric informativeness, enabling faster and more reproducible assessment of de novo generation performance.

4.4.2 Training and inference time

We further report training and inference runtime to characterise the practical cost of model optimisation and sample generation. Together with the evaluation-time acceleration above, these results provide a system-level view of computational efficiency.

Tab. 13 summarises end-to-end training time and inference time across diverse molecular datasets, reflecting the costs of model development and sample generation at the same evaluation scale. Across the settings reported here, both training and generation show favourable runtime relative to the compared baselines.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
